stories.title: The Table by the Window
stories.summary: Ayesha serves a deaf customer at the table by the window, and stops a curry meant for another table because it carried an allergen. The story separates internal customers, the colleagues who depend on your work, from external customers, and shows that adapting to a need is service while shouting at someone is not.
paragraphs: Ayesha was a waitress. She worked at a restaurant called Zaitoon. It was in Lahore, near the fabric bazaar. She worked there for six months. Saturday was the busiest day.
Her manager was Tariq. He had one golden rule. "Serve the kitchen like you serve the guests." At first Ayesha laughed. Serve the kitchen? The kitchen did not tip.

Tariq explained. "Guests pay us money. They are external customers. External means outside the business. But the chefs are customers too. They are internal customers. Internal means inside the business. They need your good work. Give them clear orders on time. Then they can serve the paying guests well. One messy ticket can spoil a whole table."

So Ayesha tried it. She wrote her tickets in big, neat letters. She told the chefs about changes early. Slowly the chefs began to trust her. Food came fast to her tables. Serve the inside well. Then the outside feels it. That was the lesson.
One Saturday tested everything.

At twelve o'clock, an old lady came in alone. Her name was Khadija. She touched her ear and smiled. "I hear very little, beta." The music was loud. Ayesha went and turned it down. Then she faced Khadija in the window light. She kept her hand away from her mouth. She spoke clearly, in a normal voice. She did not shout. Shouting changes your lip shapes. It also shames the guest.

Ayesha brought a written menu and a pen. She wrote the day's specials in big letters. Khadija pointed to the soup. She was very happy. "Most places shout at me," she said. "You spoke with your face." She stayed one hour. She left a note under her cup. "The best service in many years."

At one o'clock, a man came in a wheelchair. Ayesha stayed calm. She walked in front of him. She moved two chairs out of the way. She gave him the big table by the window. It was near the accessible washroom. Accessible means easy to use with a wheelchair. But she did not say that loudly. Some help is quiet help.
She offered to carry his tray. She did not rush him. He stayed two hours with his newspaper. He left a good tip. He asked for her name.

At two o'clock came the hardest test. A boy named Umar sat with his mother. He was about nine years old. "He is allergic to peanuts," the mother said quietly. "It is very serious. He carries an injection pen." An allergy means a food makes the body very sick. A bad allergy can even kill.

Ayesha felt afraid. But she knew her training. Ask. Write. Tell. Check. She wrote ALLERGY, PEANUT on the ticket. She wrote it in big letters. Then she went to the kitchen herself. She told the chef face to face.

The chef stopped everything. A chart hung on the kitchen wall. It was the FSA list. The FSA is the government's food safety office. Its list shows fourteen allergen foods. An allergen is a food that can
cause allergies. The chart showed them big. Peanuts. Tree nuts. Milk. Eggs. Gluten. Shellfish. Mustard. And more. He checked every ingredient in Umar's order.

"Nuts must not touch his food," the chef said. "Not from a pan. Not from a spoon. That is called cross- contamination." So he started fresh. New pan. New spoon. A separate board. No shared oil. No guessing.

Then a food runner picked up a curry. It had crushed nuts on top. It was for another table. But he walked towards Umar's side of the room. "Stop," said Ayesha. Her voice was quiet but strong. The runner froze. "It is for table nine," he said. "Probably." Probably is not good enough. Ayesha checked the ticket herself. The runner was going the wrong way. She turned him around gently. She walked him to the right table. The mother saw everything. Her eyes filled with tears. "You watched," she said. "Nobody ever watches."

That evening Tariq met the staff by the till. "Today we were calm, professional, and safe," he said. "Anyone can carry plates. Serving all people is the real work." Ayesha walked home tired and happy. Her father always said this. Serving others is worship, when the niyyah is right. Tonight it felt exactly like that. Alhamdulillah.

quiz.question: Why is shouting at a deaf customer wrong?
quiz.answer: Because deafness is not solved by volume. Shouting distorts the mouth shape so lip-reading becomes harder, it embarrasses the customer in front of others, and it draws attention to their disability instead of meeting the need. The correct response is to face them, speak clearly at normal volume, reduce background noise and offer written information.

quiz.question: The curry was for another table. Why was Ayesha still right to stop it?
quiz.answer: Because it carried an allergen and would have made someone ill. Safety is one of the three needs every customer shares, so it comes before whose table the dish belonged to. Stopping an unsafe dish is never the wrong call.

quiz.question: Give one example of an internal customer and one of an external customer.
quiz.answer: Internal: a colleague such as a commis chef or the housekeeping team. External: a diner, hotel guest or (LRN's example) a taxi driver.

quiz.question: List four ways employees provide effective customer service.
quiz.answer: Any four: prompt greeting with a smile; professional appearance; product knowledge; listening and clear communication; positive body language; prompt service and kept promises; calm complaint handling; going the extra mile.

quiz.question: Name three correct adaptations for a customer with hearing issues.
quiz.answer: Any three: face them so they can lip-read; speak clearly without shouting; reduce background noise; written menus or pen and paper; be patient; hearing loops.

quiz.question: Name three ways to serve a customer with mobility issues at the venue.
quiz.answer: Any three: ramps and accessible entrances; lifts; clear walkways; a spacious convenient table; accessible toilets and rooms; offer to carry trays or luggage; never rush them.

quiz.question: How many allergens are on the FSA list? Name two.
quiz.answer: Fourteen. Any two of: celery, cereals containing gluten, crustaceans, eggs, fish, lupin, milk, molluscs, mustard, peanuts, sesame, soya, sulphur dioxide, tree nuts.

stories.title: The Ramp and the Loop
stories.summary: Areeba fixes an accessible room in ten minutes but leaves the website still saying the hotel has no step-free access, and a review three days later proves the information mattered as much as the ramp. The story covers meet-and-greet, appearance, product knowledge, hearing loops and the first step of complaint handling, which is to listen.
paragraphs: Areeba was nineteen. Tonight was her first shift alone on reception. Reception is the welcome desk of a hotel. The hotel was Hotel Shalimar, in Multan. It had a marble floor and sixty rooms.

Her manager was Hamid. Before he left, he gave her three rules. "Stand and greet guests in five seconds. Know the hotel very well. Know the rooms, the food, the prices. And when a guest is angry, listen. Stay quiet until they finish." Areeba fixed her uniform. Clean scarf. Straight name badge. Washed hands. Guests judge what they can see.

At seven, an old gentleman came to the desk. His name was Nabeel. He tapped his hearing aid. A hearing aid is a small machine in the ear. It helps a person hear. Areeba smiled. She pressed a small button by the desk sign. The sign showed an ear with a curved line. It was the hearing loop. A hearing loop sends her voice into his hearing aid. It cuts out the lobby noise. No shouting. No shame.
Nabeel's face changed. "Ah," he said softly. "You have a loop. I heard every word." He booked dinner for eight o'clock. It was easy, like for any other guest.

At eight, the doors opened hard. A woman walked in fast. Her name was Sadia. Behind her came her old mother. The mother walked slowly with a walking frame. "I booked an accessible room on the ground floor," Sadia said. Her voice got louder. "A room my mother can use easily. Your paper says second floor. My mother cannot climb stairs. I phoned twice. I looked at your website for access information. There was nothing. Do you even think?"
Areeba's ears felt hot. She wanted to explain. But she remembered Hamid's rule. She listened to every word. She did not speak. She wrote notes. This is step one with an angry guest. First, listen.
When Sadia finished, Areeba spoke quietly. "You are right. I am sorry. This is our mistake. Give me ten minutes to fix it." That was step two. Say sorry, and mean it.

Then came step three. Act. Fix the problem fast. Areeba found an accessible room on the ground floor. It had a wide door and a walk-in bathroom. She called the porter. He met the mother at the side entrance. The side entrance had a ramp. A ramp is a slope instead of steps. So there were no steps at all. Areeba walked ahead. She held the doors open. She carried the small bags herself. She did not rush the old lady. Not once.

At nine, Areeba did step four. Most staff skip this step. It is called the follow up. You go back and check the guest is happy. She phoned the room. "Is everything comfortable for your mother? Is the bathroom alright?" Sadia paused. "Yes. It is perfect, actually." Areeba sent up mint tea and an extra pillow. Nobody asked her to. She left a note for the breakfast team. Table near the door. No steps. A chair with arms.

Hamid came back. Areeba told him everything, even the hard part. "Sadia looked at our website. She wanted access information. That means facts about ramps and easy rooms. Our website has nothing. So she could not ask for help before her visit." Hamid nodded slowly. "Then that is our real fault, not the room."

That night they wrote an Accessibility page together. It listed the ramp and the hearing loop. It listed the accessible rooms. It gave a number to call before a visit. Next morning it went on the website and

Three days later, a review appeared online. "The hotel made a mistake with our booking. But a young receptionist listened. She said sorry. She fixed it in ten minutes. Then she phoned to check on my mother. We will come back." Hamid printed the review. He pinned it in the staff room. Under it he wrote one line. "Complaints do not lose guests. Bad handling does."

quiz.question: Why is a hearing loop better than a loud voice?
quiz.answer: Because a hearing loop transmits sound directly to a hearing aid, cutting out background noise, so the customer hears clearly without anyone raising their voice. It preserves dignity and privacy, and it works consistently rather than depending on which member of staff is on the desk.

quiz.question: Areeba fixed the room in ten minutes. So why did the website page still matter?
quiz.answer: Because a customer with a mobility need plans the trip before they arrive. If the website says there is no step-free access, they never book at all, so the fixed room is never seen. Accurate published information is part of accessibility, not an extra.

quiz.question: Which LRN sample answer is the external customer: commis chef or taxi driver?
quiz.answer: The taxi driver. The commis chef is internal.

quiz.question: What are the four steps of handling a complaint, in order?
quiz.answer: Listen, apologise, act, follow up.

quiz.question: What is a hearing loop, and where should one be installed?
quiz.answer: A small sound system that sends the speaker's voice straight into a hearing aid, cutting background noise. Install at reception desks and entry/exit points.

quiz.question: What should a business publish online for customers with mobility issues, and why?
quiz.answer: Access information (ramps, loops, accessible rooms, a contact number) on the website and social media, so support can be requested ahead of the visit.

quiz.question: What is cross-contamination, and how does a kitchen prevent it for an allergy order?
quiz.answer: Allergens transferring between foods through shared pans, spoons, boards or oil. Prevent it with separate, clean equipment and surfaces for the allergy order, and by checking with the chef.

stories.title: The Biryani That Waited Too Long
stories.summary: A pot of biryani is left standing after service and gives bacteria everything they need. The story walks through handler hygiene, the 5 to 63 degree danger zone, the four conditions bacteria need to grow, and cross-contamination, then counts what the business and the chef each lose when it goes wrong.
paragraphs: Salman was a junior cook. He worked at a big restaurant called Shahi Darbar. Anwar was the head chef there. Anwar ran a careful kitchen. Rules were on every wall. Blue plasters were in every first-aid box.
"Why blue?" Salman asked one day. He held one up to the light.
"No food is blue," said Anwar. "If it falls in the rice, you can see it. Nature does not make blue food. So we make our mistakes blue. Always cover a cut. A cut is full of germs."

"We call them bacteria," said Anwar. "They are tiny living things. They are far too small to see. You cannot smell them. You cannot taste them. Food can look perfect and still be full of them. Some kinds make people very ill."
"With numbers," said Anwar. "Say this one. Five to sixty-three."
"Five to sixty-three, chef."
"That is called the danger zone. Between 5 and 63 degrees, bacteria grow very fast. Colder than 5 degrees, they almost stop. Hotter than 63 degrees, most of them die."
Then Anwar held up four fingers.

"Bacteria need four things to grow. Warmth. Moisture, which means wet food. Food, like meat or rice. And time." He folded one finger down. "Take one away and they grow slowly. Which one can we take away here?"
Salman thought. "Warmth, chef. And time."
"Good boy. The other two are the dinner itself. We cannot remove rice from rice."
Anwar pointed at the rice sacks. "And learn one name. Bacillus cereus. It hides in cooked rice. It wakes up when the rice sits warm for hours."
The kitchen had boards in different colours. Red was for raw meat only. Green was for vegetables. Anwar explained this on Salman's first day.
"Germs from raw meat must never touch salad. We do not cook salad again. When germs move like that, we call it cross-contamination."
One Friday, Anwar went to his nephew's nikah. The second chef called in sick that same morning. Salman was twenty-two years old. He ran the kitchen with two juniors. There were too many orders.

Then the small shortcuts started. A junior cut cucumber on the red board. The red board was only for raw meat. Salman saw it from the other side of the kitchen. He opened his mouth to speak. Then a new order printed. Then a pan started to burn. The moment passed. He said nothing.

The lunch biryani was ready at noon. Sixty plates, golden and perfect. The hot cupboard was full. So the big pot went beside the warm stove. It was not hot. It was not cold. It was just warm. It just waited.
Rice. Warmth. Moisture. And six long hours of time.
At six, the dinner guests ate that biryani. They said it was very good. One family took a photo of the pot.

At midnight the phone began to ring. It did not stop. Eleven guests were sick all night. They vomited. They had bad stomach pain. One was a pregnant woman. She went to hospital. Her husband shouted at the night manager on the phone. The manager had no answers.
Salman heard the news at seven in the morning. He felt sick with fear. He never wanted to hurt anybody. Not once in his life.
But bacteria do not ask about intentions.

A man came on Monday morning. His name was Naveed. He was an Environmental Health Officer. People say EHO for short. An EHO works for the council. He checks that food places are safe. He can walk in at any time. He does not need to phone first. The kitchen was not even open yet.
Naveed was quiet, slow and careful. He did not shout. He just looked, and he wrote.

He asked for the fridge logs. Friday's boxes were empty. Nobody had signed them. He tested the red board. He found cucumber on it. He asked for the temperature record of the biryani. There was none. He asked how long the pot stood by the stove. Nobody could say.
Then he talked to Salman alone. The owner waited outside the door.

Salman told the truth. All of it. He saw the cucumber on the red board and said nothing. He left the pot by the stove because the hot cupboard was full. His father taught him to be honest, years ago, in a much smaller kitchen. A lie will bury you deeper, beta. Your aakhirah too.
Naveed wrote it all down. He thanked Salman for the truth.

For the restaurant: an improvement notice. An improvement notice is a legal letter from the council. It lists what you must fix. It gives you a date. Every worker had to be trained again. The rules had to be rebuilt. There was a big deep clean before the doors opened again.

The hygiene rating fell to one star. A hygiene rating is a score for safety and cleaning. It goes from zero stars to five stars. By law, the restaurant had to show it in the front window. Every customer walked past it. Bookings stopped inside one week.

Then the sick guest asked the restaurant to pay for her hospital care. The owner paid fines to the court too. The fines ate one whole year of profit. He paid from the money he had saved for his daughter's school.

For Salman: a disciplinary meeting in the office upstairs. A disciplinary meeting is a serious meeting about your mistakes. You can lose your job in one. He sat on a plastic chair. He listened to his own mistakes read out loud. He kept his job, but only just. He kept it because he told the truth. He kept it because he agreed to full training again. The two juniors were trained again beside him. He did not sleep well for a month.
Anwar came back. He did not shout either. That felt worse.
He rebuilt everything with a system called HACCP. The letters mean Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points.

"It sounds hard. It is simple," Anwar said. "We look at every step, from the delivery van to the plate. We ask what could go wrong. We pick the step where we must control it. We set a number. We check the number. We write it down."

Every danger went on a chart on the office wall. Every important step got a number, a check and a signature. Cooked rice: cool it fast inside ninety minutes, or hold it above sixty-three degrees. Write the number. Sign it. Check it twice each service. Handwashing checks too.

The probes were tested every Monday. A probe is a thermometer for food. You push it into the middle of the food and read the number. Testing a probe is called calibration. It makes sure the number is true. Supplier papers went in a red folder with the date on the spine.
Six months of perfect logs went by. Then Naveed came back with no warning. He stayed three hours. He left. The new rating came by post.
Five stars. Anwar hung it in the window himself. Then he called the team together under it at closing time.

"This paper is not the prize," he said. "The prize is every guest who goes home well. They sleep. They wake up. They never think about us at all. We look after their health. Al-Ameen means the trustworthy one. There is no better name in this work."
Salman looked at the certificate for a long moment. Then he went and checked the fridge log one more time. He had already signed it.

quiz.question: Name the bacteria that loves warm cooked rice. Which four conditions is that pot giving it right now?
quiz.answer: Bacillus cereus, which is associated with cooked rice left at room temperature. The pot is giving it warmth because it is standing in the danger zone, food because rice is a nutrient source, moisture from the cooking, and time because it has been left for hours.

quiz.answer: The business lost the food itself, its custom through bad reviews, and money through refunds, closure or prosecution. Salman lost his job and his professional reputation. The reputation damage hurt the owner most, because food and money can be replaced but a name for unsafe food keeps customers away long afterwards.

quiz.question: Define food hygiene in one sentence.
quiz.answer: The practices that keep food, people, equipment and premises clean and free from contamination.

quiz.question: Give the danger zone as a range.
Which bacteria is linked to cooked rice left at room temperature?
quiz.answer: **Bacillus cereus.**

quiz.question: How long must a food handler stay off work after sickness or diarrhoea?
quiz.answer: **48 hours after the symptoms have stopped.**

quiz.question: Give two consequences for a business operator who breaks food safety law.
quiz.answer: Any two: improvement notice, prohibition notice, emergency closure, prosecution, unlimited fines, imprisonment, low hygiene rating displayed publicly, compensation claims, brand damage or closure.

stories.title: Madiha's Red Folder
stories.summary: Madiha's red folder is a food safety management system based on HACCP, and it saves the business when inspector Parveen arrives. The story shows hazard analysis, critical control points with measurable limits, the handler's duty to refuse an unsafe instruction, and why an inspector asks for paperwork before looking at any food.
paragraphs: Madiha bought the old café on Jail Road. She paid very little for it. There was a reason. The council closed the last owner down. His food made people ill. The whole street knew the story, and nobody forgot it.
Her brother said she was mad. Her mother said, sell tea from home instead. Madiha signed the papers anyway. Then she stood alone in the empty kitchen with a notebook.
She gave Shafiq the head chef job because of one answer in his interview. She asked him a question. What would he do if she told him to serve food he thought was unsafe?
"I would say no, madam," he said. "Politely. Once. And then I would say no again."
She gave him the job that day.
They did not open for six weeks. They built the system first.
Shafiq walked her round the kitchen slowly. Delivery door. Store room. Fridge. Prep table. Stove. Pass. At every place he asked one question. What could go wrong here?
"A thing that can go wrong is called a hazard," he said. "The way we stop it is called a control. Every control needs a number, or nobody can check it."
Madiha wrote every answer in a red folder.

Delivery. The hazard: food arrives too warm, or from a shop nobody can trace. The control: check the temperature of every cold delivery at the door. Buy from two named suppliers only, with proper papers.
Store room. The hazard: old food hides at the back and goes bad. The control: FIFO. It means first in, first out. The oldest food sits at the front. It gets used first. Every shelf has a date label.
Fridge. The hazard: it gets warm and nobody sees. The control: read it morning and evening. Write the number. Sign it. Keep it between 0 and 5 degrees.

Cooking. The hazard: chicken looks cooked but is still raw inside. The control: use a probe. A probe is a thermometer for food. Push it into the thickest part. It must read 75 degrees. Then write it down.
"All this has a name," said Shafiq. "It is called HACCP. The letters mean Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. People think it is a big frightening thing. It is only this folder."

Madiha spent money on things guests never see. She bought two probes. She checked both in a jug of iced water on the first Monday of every month. This check is called calibration. It proves the probe tells the truth.
A pest control man came every month. He killed mice and flies, and he left a signed sheet. Mice and flies carry germs onto food.

She put in a proper handwash basin, with soap and paper towels. It was away from the sink for washing vegetables. She bought blue plasters for cuts. She bought boards in different colours, one colour for each kind of food.

She trained all six staff herself over two evenings. Then she did one more thing. She made every person sign a training sheet with the date on it. Shafiq watched her put the sheets in the red folder. He nodded slowly.
"Most owners train their staff," he said. "Few of them can prove it."
Then came a test she did not expect.

Two weeks after opening, a young waiter phoned her at six in the morning. He sounded shy. He was sick twice in the night. He felt fine now, he said. He could come to work. It was Saturday. The café was fully booked. He did not want to let her down.
Madiha felt worried. Saturday. Full. And two staff already missing.
"When did the sickness stop?" she asked.
"About three in the morning."

"Then I will see you on Monday evening," she said. "The rule is forty-eight hours after the sickness stops. Not forty-eight hours after it starts. Your body still carries the germs when you feel completely well. We call those germs bacteria. They can go from your hands into the food. Rest at home. I will still pay you."
She put the phone down. Then she served the tables herself all day, in a dupatta and an apron. Her feet hurt by night.

A woman came on a Tuesday morning with no warning. Her name was Parveen. She was an Environmental Health Officer, or EHO. An EHO works for the council. She checks that food places are safe. She can come at any time, with no appointment.

She asked for four things before she even took her coat off. The food safety management system, which means the written plan for keeping food safe. The training records. The temperature logs. The allergen information.
Madiha gave her the red folder.

Parveen read it for forty minutes. She checked the fridge and it matched the log. She asked a kitchen porter to show her how he washed his hands. He did it correctly, and he did not stop to think. She looked behind the stove and under the shelves. She found nothing bad.

Then she asked Shafiq about allergens. Some people become very ill from one food. That food is called an allergen for them. The law names fourteen of these foods. A café must tell guests which ones are in each dish.
"Name three," said Parveen.
"Gluten, shellfish and mustard," said Shafiq. He pointed at the allergen chart on the wall beside the menu.
Then Parveen found the note about the sick waiter. It had the date on it. The return date was written beside it.
She tapped the note with one finger. "Most people get this one wrong," she said. "They send the person back the next day."
Then Parveen gave the café its hygiene rating. A hygiene rating is a score for safety and cleaning. Five stars is the best. The café must show it in the window.
Madiha did not put the certificate in the window at once. She took it home first. She showed her mother. Her mother cried a little, then said she had not.
That night she closed up alone. She ran her hand along the red folder on the shelf. Six weeks of work with no money coming in. At the time it felt like madness.
Alhamdulillah for those six weeks, she thought. Then she turned off the light.

quiz.question: Look at the fridge step. What is the hazard? What is the control? What number is the limit?
quiz.answer: The hazard is bacterial growth in high-risk food. The control is refrigerated storage, with the temperature monitored and recorded. The limit is 0 to 5 degrees Celsius, because above 5 the food enters the danger zone.

quiz.question: Parveen asked for four papers before she looked at any food. Why does an inspector start with paperwork and not with the kitchen?
quiz.answer: Because the paperwork shows whether food safety is managed all the time or only on the day of the visit. Records of temperatures, cleaning, training and deliveries reveal the system behind the kitchen, and a clean kitchen with no records proves nothing about yesterday or last week.

quiz.question: What does "pathogenic" mean?
quiz.answer: Disease-causing.

quiz.question: Name the four conditions bacteria need to multiply.
quiz.answer: Warmth, moisture, food and time.

quiz.question: Which pathogenic bacteria can still grow inside a fridge, and who is most at risk from it?
quiz.answer: **Listeria**, and pregnant women are most at risk.

quiz.question: What does HACCP stand for?
quiz.answer: **Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points.**

quiz.question: What does FIFO mean, and why does it matter?
quiz.answer: **First in, first out.** Older stock is used first, so nothing sits at the back of a shelf past its date.

stories.title: Talha and the Numbers on the Wall
stories.lesson_title: Cook It, Hold It, Chill It
stories.summary: Talha learns the cooking methods and the numbers written on the kitchen wall: braising, stewing, roasting at 170 to 185 degrees with added fat, and baking without it. The story also explains why leftovers go into shallow trays and why they are stirred while cooling.
paragraphs: There was a board on the wall at Almas Restaurant. It hung above the pass. The pass is the counter where finished food waits for the waiters. Three numbers were painted on the board. They were big and white on black.
Talha was new. He was nineteen. On his first morning he tied his apron and stared at the board.
Chef Bashir tapped the board with his spoon. He did not look up.
"These three numbers are your shield. Learn them before you learn recipes. Recipes change. These numbers never change."
The morning was a cooking lesson. Bashir taught while he walked.
First the lamb. He cooked it in a hot pan until it was brown. Then he put it in a pot with a little stock. He put the lid on. He pushed the pot to the back of the stove for three hours.
"This is called braising," he said. "Look at the liquid. Only a little. It comes halfway up the meat. The lid stays on."
"And if you use more liquid, chef?"
"Then it is stewing. In stewing, liquid covers the food completely. And we serve that liquid with the dish. Small difference in the pot. Big difference in the exam."
Next the whole chickens went into the oven. Bashir spooned melted ghee over the skin two times. Then he shut the door.
"This is roasting. Hot dry air in an oven, and fat on top of the food. The oven is at 170 to 185 degrees. Fat on, colour on."
The bread went in beside the chickens. The potatoes went in plain and dry on a tray.
"This is baking. Dry heat in an oven, and nothing added on top. Same oven, Talha. Same air. One difference." He held up the ghee spoon. "This."
Then he turned on the salamander. A salamander is a grill with very strong heat above the food. The steaks and the sausages went under it. They hissed.
"This is grilling. The heat shines straight onto the food. We call it radiant heat. It is fast. It suits soft, tender meat."
Talha watched the fat drip through the bars into the tray below.
"Look at that fat. It leaves the food. That is why grilling is the healthiest of these methods."
Then fish went into a wide shallow pan of liquid. The liquid shook a little. It never bubbled.
"This is poaching. Gentle and slow. About seventy-five degrees, never boiling. Boiling breaks a soft fillet into pieces."
The vegetables sat in a basket above the water. They were bright and firm.
"This is steaming. The food sits above the water, not in it. The steam cooks it. It keeps the colour and the goodness."
Then the mussels. They rattled inside a covered pot. Bashir shook the pot hard. He waited. He lifted the lid.
Most shells were wide open. Three stayed shut.
He picked out those three and dropped them in the bin.
"Open means cooked. Closed means never serve it. That rule has no exceptions and no bad days."
Then came the first number: 75.

Talha carried a probe in his top pocket, like a pen, because Bashir carried his that way. A probe is a thermometer for food. He wiped it clean. He pushed it into the thickest part of a chicken thigh. He waited for the number to stop moving.

"Safe," said Bashir. "Food must reach 75 degrees in the middle. We call that the core temperature. The middle is the last part to get hot. The outside can be 90 degrees while the middle is still 55. Only the middle kills the germs."
He pointed at the chicken.
"And chicken is never served pink. Never. Not for a guest. Not for the owner. Not for his father. If a guest asks for pink chicken, you say no. Then you say no again."
Lunch service started. With it came the second number: 63.
At the front of the restaurant there was a carvery. A carvery is a long hot counter. Roast meat sits there under hot lamps, and guests come for slices. The lamps glowed orange over the roast lamb.
At two o'clock Talha remembered the board. He took the probe out to the lamb.

Bashir came out fast. He wiped his hands. He did not argue with the number. He put his palm under the lamp. He felt nothing. The bulb died quietly some time in the last hour. Nobody saw it, because the meat still looked warm and golden.

"Hot food must stay at 63 degrees or above," said Bashir. "That is called hot holding. Under 63 degrees, food falls into the danger zone. The danger zone is 5 to 63 degrees. Germs grow fast in there."
The lamb was in the danger zone now. For how long? Twenty minutes? Ninety? Nobody could say.
The manager came to Bashir's elbow. "It is only three degrees, chef. Just turn the lamp up."

"Three degrees is not the problem. The problem is the time. I do not know the time. And I cannot serve 'I do not know' to a family." He picked up the tray himself. "We lose one tray of lamb. Or we risk forty stomachs. That is not a real choice, beta."
The tray went in the bin. A new bulb went in that afternoon. A checklist went up beside the lamps. Check every joint every hour. Write the number. Sign it.
The evening brought the third number: 90.
There was a big pot of haleem for tomorrow. Talha started to carry it to the cold room. Bashir stopped him with two fingers on the rim.
"You are carrying a heater into a fridge. Hot food warms everything in there."

So Talha ladled the haleem into shallow trays, in a thin layer. He stood the trays in the sink in iced water. He stirred each one every few minutes. The steam went first. Then the warmth went. Inside one hour the trays were cool enough to hold. He covered them. He wrote a label for each one, with the date.
"Hot food must cool inside ninety minutes," said Bashir. "Then it goes in the fridge. That is the third number."
He pointed at the empty pot.
"That deep pot keeps its heat until midnight. The middle stays warm all night. Shallow trays and a spoon let the heat escape fast. Same haleem. Same kitchen. One way is safe. One way is a hospital."
At closing time Bashir untied his apron and tested him quickly.
Bashir smiled properly for the first time that day.

"My teacher made me say these like times tables. I hated him for it. I have cooked for thirty years. No guest of mine ever got sick. Not one. That is my real wealth, Alhamdulillah. I did not build it with talent. I built it with three numbers on a wall."
He hung up his apron. He looked back from the door.
"Guard your record from tonight, Talha. It stays perfect only if it starts perfect."

quiz.question: Roasting and baking both use an oven. Both use dry heat. Say the one difference between them.
quiz.answer: Added fat. Roasting uses hot dry air in an oven with added fat at about 170 to 185 degrees, which browns the outside; baking uses dry heat in the oven without adding fat over the food.

quiz.question: Why shallow trays? Why stirring? Say what each one does to the heat.
quiz.answer: Shallow trays spread the food thinly so heat escapes from a much larger surface and the centre is never far from the outside, which cools it fast. Stirring keeps moving the hot food from the middle to the outside so heat is released instead of being trapped in the centre.

quiz.question: Define roasting, including its temperature range.
quiz.answer: Cooking in an oven with hot dry air and **added fat**, at **170-185°C**, giving a browned outside and tender inside.

quiz.question: Define grilling, and say why it is considered a healthier method.
quiz.answer: Fast cooking by **direct radiant heat** from above or below. Healthier because the fat drains away from the food.

quiz.question: Define braising in the words the mark scheme uses.
quiz.answer: Slow cooking in a **small amount of liquid** in a covered pot.

quiz.question: State the minimum hot-holding temperature for hot food.
quiz.answer: **63°C or above.**

quiz.question: After cooking, what do you do with a shellfish whose shell has stayed closed?
quiz.answer: Throw it away. A shell that stays closed after cooking is not safe to serve.

stories.title: The Sunday Carvery at the Grand Nishat
stories.lesson_title: Cook It, Hold It, Chill It
stories.summary: At a Sunday carvery, chicken on hot hold is drifting towards 63 degrees and Noman wants to wait for the next scheduled check. Rehman refuses to reheat it to 75 degrees and serve it anyway, which forces the crucial point that time spent in the danger zone causes damage reheating cannot undo.
paragraphs: Every Sunday the Grand Nishat hotel served a carvery. A carvery is a long hot counter. Big pieces of roast meat sit there under hot lamps. A chef cuts slices for the guests. Two hundred and forty people came between one and four o'clock. It was the busiest time of the hotel's week.
Noman was twenty-one. He worked on the carvery for three weeks. Chef Rehman gave him one job.

"You are not cutting the meat. You are guarding it. Check every joint with the probe every thirty minutes. Write the number down. If a number is under sixty-three, do not think about it. Do not talk about it. Call me."
A joint is one big piece of roast meat. A probe is a thermometer for food.
"Sixty-three, chef. Hot food must be held at sixty-three degrees or above."
At half past twelve the joints came out of the ovens. Rehman checked each one in front of Noman, so the boy could watch him do it.

"Beef. Seventy-eight. Lamb. Seventy-nine. Now the chicken. I push the probe into the thickest part of the thigh." He waited for the number to settle. "Seventy-nine. Every food must reach 75 degrees in the middle. Chicken is never served pink, so I want it well past seventy-five."
"Chef, how hot was the oven?"
Rehman looked happy with the question.

"170 to 185 degrees. That is the roasting range. Roasting means dry oven heat with fat spooned over the meat. The fat is what makes it roasting and not baking. Baking is the same dry oven heat, but with no fat on top."
He pointed at the cold table.

"Those prawns were poached. Poaching means cooking gently in liquid, at about seventy-five degrees. The liquid never boils." He shut the oven door. "Numbers, Noman. This work runs on numbers, not on how food looks."
Service opened at one o'clock. It went well for ninety minutes.
At half past two Noman took his readings. Beef, 68. Lamb, 71. Chicken, 64.
Sixty-four. That was still above sixty-three. But half an hour before, it was 72.
He did not wait. He knelt down and looked under the counter. He saw it at once. A plug hung half out of the socket. A trolley knocked it in the rush. Two of the eight heaters were dead.
Rehman came at a walk, not a run. A running chef frightens the guests. He read the log over Noman's shoulder. Seventy-two, then sixty-four. Twenty-eight minutes between the two numbers.
He pushed the plug back in. The heaters ticked and started to warm.
Then Arsalan came. Arsalan was the banquet manager. He had a queue of forty people. He also had a big function in the ballroom at four.
"The chicken has been falling for half an hour," said Rehman. "It is at sixty-four."
"Sixty-four is above sixty-three."
"It is above sixty-three now. I put the plug back one minute ago. I do not know the number at twenty past two. Nobody was looking then. It could be sixty. It could be fifty-eight."
Arsalan spoke quietly. "Chef. Forty people are waiting. The beef and the lamb are fine. Take the chicken off and we have no chicken for an hour. On a Sunday. In front of the whole city."
Rehman was quiet for a moment. Noman watched him and held his breath.
"Take the chicken off," said Rehman. "Now."
"Chef, please be reasonable."

"I am being reasonable. Say I serve that chicken. Say one family gets ill. Then the EHO comes. The EHO is the council inspector for food. He gives us a low hygiene rating. That rating is a score, and by law it hangs in our window for the whole city to read. Then your ballroom booking next Sunday cancels itself. You want me to save one hour and risk the whole year."
Arsalan stood there. Then he nodded once. He went and spoke to the queue himself. Later, Noman thought that was a kind thing to do.
The chicken tray came off the counter. It did not go back in the oven to get hot again. Rehman did not want to guess how long it sat below the line.
But it did not go in the bin either, not yet. That surprised Noman.

"That joint came out of the oven at seventy-nine degrees. No customer touched it. But it sat too cool on the counter. So I will not hold it hot and I will not serve it hot. Heating it again makes it hot. It does not make it safe. Some germs leave behind a poison, and heat does not kill that poison. But I am not going to guess either. Blast chiller. Now."
The blast chiller was a tall steel cabinet at the back of the kitchen. It blows very cold air hard over the food inside. Noman had hardly used it.
Rehman cut the joint into thin slices. He spread them on a shallow tray. He slid the tray inside.

"Whole and deep, this meat takes four hours to cool. Every one of those hours sits inside the danger zone, 5 to 63 degrees. Sliced thin, in this machine, it drops from seventy-something to under five degrees in ninety minutes. That is the job of a blast chiller. Ninety minutes, from hot to cold, straight through the danger zone."
He wrote the start time on the tray with a marker. 14:41.
"And tomorrow, chef? Do we use it?"

"Tomorrow I will read the cooling log and the holding log side by side. Then I will decide. Records first, opinions second. If the two logs do not convince me, it goes in the bin, and I sleep well tonight."
At four o'clock the service closed. Two hundred and forty guests. Nobody noticed anything, except one hour with no chicken.
Rehman signed Noman's holding log and gave it back.
"You caught it at sixty-four," he said. "Not at fifty. Sixty-four. That is the whole job. And nobody in that room will ever know you did it."
Noman looked at the sheet. It was a column of small numbers in his own handwriting.
"Chef, can I ask you something? What if I did not look under the counter? What if I just wrote sixty-four and went back to work?"
Rehman took a long breath.

"Then at three o'clock the meat is at fifty-five. At half past three it goes onto two hundred plates. And on Wednesday you and I sit in the office with a man from the council. He has a list of names of people in hospital." He put a hand on Noman's shoulder. "You are twenty-one. You will do this work for forty years. Every day some number will be a little low. Nobody will be watching you. What you do in that second is who you are."
Noman went home that evening. He did not tell anybody what happened, because nothing happened.

quiz.question: The chicken is still above 63 degrees. So it is safe right now. What should Noman do? Why should he not just wait for the next check?
quiz.answer: He should act now: reheat it to 75 degrees or above, or discard it, and record what he did. He should not wait for the next scheduled check because hot holding must stay at 63 degrees or above at all times, and by the next check the food may have spent an unknown length of time below it.

quiz.question: Rehman did not heat the chicken back up to 75 degrees and serve it. Say why. What does time in the danger zone do that heating cannot fix?
quiz.answer: Because the chicken had already spent time in the danger zone, and during that time bacteria multiplied and produced heat-stable toxins. Reheating to 75 degrees kills the bacteria but does not destroy the toxins they have already made, so the food can still cause illness.

quiz.question: What is the single difference between roasting and baking?
quiz.answer: The **added fat over the food**. Roasting has it, baking does not.

quiz.question: At roughly what temperature is food poached?
quiz.answer: Around **75°C**, gently, below boiling.

quiz.question: State the core temperature food must reach when cooked.
quiz.answer: **75°C** core (or 70°C held for 2 minutes).

quiz.question: Within how long must cooked food be chilled, and what machine does this job professionally?
quiz.answer: Within **90 minutes**; a **blast chiller**.

quiz.question: Why does reheating unsafe food to 75°C not make it safe?
quiz.answer: Because bacteria multiplied during the time it spent in the danger zone, and some of them produce toxins that heat does not destroy. Reheating makes food hot, not safe.

stories.title: Grandmother Safia's Five Baskets
stories.summary: Grandmother Safia lays out five baskets of food and shows what each one gives the body. The story explains protein, iron, vitamins, minerals and fibre through what happens when they are missing, using Zainab's anaemia and the sailors' scurvy as the two named deficiency diseases.
paragraphs: Zainab came home pale and tired again. It was the third time this month. She dropped her bag. She lay down. Her mother felt her forehead. She looked worried.
The doctor's note was on the table. It said low iron. Iron is a mineral in food. It makes blood strong. The note also said mild anaemia. Anaemia is an illness. It means weak, tired blood.
"But I eat a lot," said Zainab.

Grandmother Safia folded her prayer mat slowly. "You eat a lot of the same thing," she said. "Biscuits, chips, bread. Your plate has only one colour, beti. Come to the bazaar tomorrow. Bring five baskets. I will show you real food."
"You will count them yourself."
They walked to the bazaar at dawn. The stalls were just opening. "Food is full of nutrients, beti," said Safia. "Nutrients are the good things inside food. Your body needs them to work."

Basket one was at the butcher's stall. Mutton and beef, red and fresh. "Look at this red colour, beti. This red colour is iron. Iron makes your blood strong. You are tired because your blood needs iron." Safia touched the meat gently. "Meat gives protein too. Protein is the nutrient that builds your body. It helps you grow and repair. Meat also gives zinc and vitamin B12. But listen. Meat fat is the heavy kind. It is called saturated fat. Too much is bad for the heart. So do not eat too much meat."

Basket two filled up with colour. Carrots and potatoes are root vegetables. Spinach and broccoli are leafy vegetables. Tomatoes and peppers are fruiting vegetables. Lentils and peas are legumes. "Four families of vegetables," said Safia. "Root, leafy, fruiting, legume. They give vitamins and minerals. Vitamins and minerals are tiny helpers in food. They protect your health. Vegetables give fibre too. Fibre is the rough part of plants. It helps food move through your body. Vegetables have almost no fat. Your grandfather eats many vegetables. That is why he is still strong."
Basket three was at the poultry stall. They bought a chicken and some turkey. "Chicken is lean protein. Lean means low in fat. It is lighter than red meat. It is good for every day."

The fish-seller filled basket four. First white fish, cod and plaice. Then silver mackerel, an oily fish. "There are two kinds of fish, beti. White fish has very little fat. Oily fish keeps fat in its flesh. That fat has omega-3. Omega-3 is a special good fat. It protects the heart. It helps the brain too. Oily fish also gives vitamins A and D."
Basket five held prawns, crabs and mussels. "Shellfish are small treasure chests. They give zinc, iodine, selenium and iron. Low fat, but full of minerals."
They walked home. The baskets felt heavy. Zainab asked her big question. "Dadi, why five baskets? Why not just one?"
Safia stopped in the lane. "No single food gives you everything. Protein repairs your body. Carbohydrates give you energy. Good fats keep you warm. They also carry vitamins into your body.
Vitamins and minerals protect you. Fibre moves your digestion. Water carries it all."
"Now think, beti. Eat only one food, and something is missing. Miss it for months, and you get ill. Your low iron is a small warning."
"Can the warning get bigger?"

"Much bigger. Long ago, sailors ate only biscuits and salted meat. They had no vegetables for months. So they had no vitamin C. Their gums started to bleed. Their cuts did not heal. That illness is called scurvy. Doctors call illnesses like this deficiency diseases. Deficiency means something is missing. One missing nutrient made strong men ill. Allah put health in many foods. So eat many foods."

Three months later, Zainab looked healthy again. The doctor was happy with her results. That evening Zainab cooked for the family. Mutton with spinach, lentils, warm bread, tomatoes. She named each nutrient as she served. "Iron for blood. Fibre for digestion. Protein for repair." Safia laughed with joy. "My student. Alhamdulillah. Now teach your brother."

stories.title: The Pantry Before the Snow
stories.summary: Before the snow closes the road for months, a family fills the pantry using drying, salting, pickling, bottling and freezing. The story is a comparison of preservation methods and their effect on nutrients: which ones keep vitamins, which destroy vitamin C, and why frozen vegetables can beat days-old fresh ones.
paragraphs: Haroon ran a small hotel in the mountains. It had fourteen rooms and wood stoves. Every winter the road below closed. Sometimes for two weeks. Sometimes for two months. Then there was no market. There were no deliveries. Only the pantry fed everyone. A pantry is a food store room.
Laiba was his new assistant. She came from Lahore. This was her first mountain October. Haroon gave her a long list. "We fill the pantry before the snow. This food must feed our guests till spring."
Laiba read the list. "Then let us buy fresh spinach," she said. "Fresh tomatoes. Fresh everything."
Haroon smiled. "Fresh spinach goes bad in ten days. Fresh food spoils fast. We need food that can wait."

He showed her the store room. "We can preserve food. Preserving means treating food so it lasts longer. It gives food a long shelf life. Shelf life is how long food stays safe. There are five ways. Watch what each way costs."

On the roof, apricots dried in the sun. There were many trays of them. "Drying takes the water out. Microbes are tiny germs. They cannot live without water. So the fruit lasts for months. But the sugar gets stronger. And some vitamin C is gone. Vitamin C is a nutrient. Nutrients are the good things in food. Sweet, but not the same."

In the back room stood a big freezer. It held peas, mixed vegetables, fish, berries. "We froze these on harvest day," said Haroon. "Cold stops food from spoiling. Freezing keeps most of the nutrients. Here is a secret. Your 'fresh' spinach travelled five days in a lorry. It lost vitamins the whole time. My peas were frozen in hours. In February, my frozen peas beat your tired fresh ones."
Laiba laughed. "The freezer beats the market?"

On a shelf sat tight silver packets. Smoked salmon, cooked meats, coffee. "These are vacuum- packed. A machine pulls the air out. With no air, food spoils slowly. And the food almost does not change. Little lost, little gained."

Next came the cured meats. They hung under a thin cloth. They were dark and salty. "Curing means keeping meat with salt. The salt pulls the water out. So the meat lasts. But the salt stays inside." He stopped. "Last winter a guest came here. He was an old doctor. He had high blood pressure. That means the blood pushes too hard inside the body. Too much salt raises blood pressure. So I could not give him cured meat every day. Cured food is a sometimes food."

Last came the wall of cans. Tomatoes, tuna, beans, peaches, many rows. "Canning seals food inside a can. Then we heat the can very hot. The heat kills the microbes. But it also kills some vitamin C. It kills some B vitamins too. The protein survives. The minerals survive. The fibre survives. In every method, the vitamins suffer most. Protein and minerals are strong. Vitamins are delicate. Delicate means they break easily."

The snow came in December. It stayed. In February a storm closed the road. It stayed closed for three weeks. But the hotel stayed warm. The plates stayed full. Lentils with canned tomatoes. Frozen vegetables with fish. Dried apricots after dinner.
One evening the doctor guest smiled. "These vegetables taste so fresh. How, in February?"
"They are frozen, sir," said Laiba. "Frozen on harvest day."
That night Haroon locked the pantry. He said Alhamdulillah quietly. A full pantry in a snowstorm is a big blessing.

stories.title: Hamza's Summer at the Pine View Hotel
stories.summary: Hamza spends a summer working at his uncle's hotel in Murree and learns the whole shape of the industry from the inside: what a product is, what a service is, who does which job, and how four very different guests in one afternoon each need something different. It ends with a near-miss over a nut allergy, which shows that missing one special need breaks the basic need to feel safe.
paragraphs: Hamza was fourteen. His summer holidays started. His mother wanted him out of bed.
His uncle Shakeel had a hotel in Murree. The hotel was called the Pine View. Uncle spoke to her on the phone. "Send him to me. He can watch. He can learn what we sell."
The bus went up the mountain. It took three hours. Hamza saw the hotel from the road. It had white walls and a green roof. Pine trees stood behind it.
It looked like a picture. Inside, it smelled clean. It smelled of fresh bread too.
On the first morning, Hamza stood at reception. A guest in a grey coat paid for a room. He counted his money slowly.
Uncle spoke quietly to Hamza. "That room is our product. A product is a thing you can buy and touch. He can sleep in it. He can touch the bed. He can lock the door."

Then Maryam smiled at the guest. Maryam was the receptionist. "Welcome to Pine View, sir," she said. She carried his bag upstairs herself. She told him about breakfast times. She showed him the qibla sticker on the ceiling.
Uncle said, "That is our service. A service is work we do for the guest. He cannot hold it. He cannot put it in his bag. But he will remember it. He will remember it longer than the bed."

That week, Hamza met the whole team. In the kitchen, the head chef was the boss. A young commis chef cut onions. A commis chef is a junior chef. He is still learning. The head chef shouted at him, but in a kind way.
A kitchen porter washed pots. A porter cleans and helps. He washed the pots until they shone. "The kitchen is back of house," said Uncle. "Guests do not see these workers."
At the front, Maryam ran the desk. A housekeeper made the rooms fresh again. A waiter carried four plates at one time. "They are front of house," said Uncle. "Guests can see them."

Upstairs, Uncle managed them all. He had a notebook and a calm voice. "Every job matters," Uncle said. "The chef cooks a perfect meal. But maybe the porter leaves one dirty pot. Then the whole kitchen fails the check. If one person is missing, the hotel falls."
The next week was hard for Hamza. Four guests came in one afternoon. Each guest needed different things.
First came a businessman. He was tired and in a hurry. "Is the Wi-Fi fast? Can breakfast come at six?" Hamza wrote it down.
Then came a family with a small baby. The mother looked very tired. "A quiet room, please. And a high chair at dinner."
Then came an old lady with a walking stick. "Ground floor, beta. My knees cannot climb stairs."
Then came a guest in a wheelchair. He needed the ramp. Bags blocked the ramp, so Hamza moved them.
Hamza ran all day. His feet hurt. But he saw something strange. Four very different guests. Four very different lists.
That evening, Hamza almost made a big mistake. A guest ordered the chicken karahi. Hamza wrote the order. He turned to go.

"Wait," said Maryam quietly. She held his sleeve. "Look at the booking notes. This guest has a nut allergy. Nuts can make her very sick. She told us this morning. Our karahi masala has ground almonds in it. Ask the chef first."
Hamza felt sick with fear. He ran to the kitchen. The chef changed the dish. No almonds. No problem.
The guest never knew about the danger. She wrote a five-star review. She called them "the kindest staff in Murree".
Hamza could not sleep that night. One missed note. One trip to hospital. Now he understood Maryam. She read every booking twice.
On his last evening, at Maghrib, Hamza sat with his uncle. They sat on the back steps. The sunset made the pine trees gold. Inside, plates made small sounds. A child laughed.

"Alhamdulillah," said Uncle Shakeel softly. "Every guest felt welcome. Every guest was safe. Every guest felt the price was fair. People call that value for money. That is hospitality, beta. Food, drink and a bed, with a warm welcome."

stories.title: One Pot of Daal, Three Kitchens
stories.summary: One dish, daal, is cooked in three different kitchens: Owais sells it for profit, Saima gives it away at a langar funded by donations, and a government hospital serves it from public money. The same food in three sectors makes the definition of commercial, voluntary and public impossible to forget, because the difference is simply who pays.
paragraphs: In one small city, three cooks made the same dish. It was a Thursday. The dish was daal chawal. Yellow daal, white rice.
Same dish, three different kitchens. Watch closely. The difference is the whole exam point.
The first kitchen belonged to Owais. His restaurant was on the main road. It had bright green lights. His daal chawal cost 350 rupees a plate.
Owais checked the money box at noon. He checked it again at three. He had to check. He had to pay rent on Friday. Six workers waited for their wages. The gas bill hung on a nail by the door.
"Every plate must make money," Owais told his waiter. "If we sell well, we all eat. If we sell badly, this shop closes forever."

His customers paid for everything. Owais worked for profit. Profit is the money left after you pay all costs. A business like his is called commercial. There was no shame in that. Profit paid wages to six families.
The second kitchen had no money box at all. It was behind the big mosque. Saima stirred a very big pot. The pot came up to her waist.
Saima was a volunteer. A volunteer works for free, to help people. This kitchen was the langar. The daal was free. The rice was free. Nobody paid even one rupee.
A traveller ate next to a worker. A widow took a bag home for her children. The money came from donations. A donation is money people give as a gift, to help. Some gave their names. Most did not.
A boy asked her, "Who pays for all this?" Saima smiled. "People who want a reward from Allah. Not money in a box. This is voluntary work. Nobody here wants profit."
At sunset she washed the big pot. She said Alhamdulillah. She was tired in a happy way.
The third kitchen was inside the government hospital. Kashif wore a hairnet. He pushed a steel trolley down long halls. Ward six, bed by bed.
His daal was softer. It had less salt. He followed a food chart for sick people. The patients paid nothing. There was no money box. There was no donation box either.
A new helper asked, "So who pays you, Kashif bhai?"

"The government," said Kashif. "Tax money. Tax is money people must pay to the government. The government uses it for hospitals like this. So this is a public kitchen. Patients must eat. It does not matter if they can pay. Nobody makes a profit. Nobody stays hungry."
He stopped at the last bed. An old man lay there. He was too weak to sit up. Kashif lifted the spoon himself. He fed the old man slowly.
That night, the city slept with full stomachs. Owais counted his profit. He paid one wage early. Saima's pot stood clean for Friday. Kashif's trolley was charging by the wall.

These three kitchens show the three sectors. A sector is one part of an industry. Commercial works for profit. Voluntary runs on donations. Public runs on government money. The exam will ask you to name all three, with an example each. Now you have three faces to remember. Not three cold words.

stories.title: The Certificate on the Wall
stories.summary: A framed certificate behind a hotel desk turns out to be membership of the Institute of Hospitality. As Mehak calmly handles four problems in a row, the story shows what a professional body does, monitoring standards, reviewing CPD and liaising on best practice, and what personal qualities the exam expects hospitality staff to display.
paragraphs: Mehak was seventeen. This was her first job. She was a waitress at the Silver Spoon banquet hall.
On her first day she saw a certificate. It hung in a frame behind the manager's desk. It had a fancy border and a gold seal. She read the words. "Institute of Hospitality. Member: Zohaib Ahmed."
"Is that a prize?" she asked.

Zohaib was her manager. He laughed. "No. It is a promise. The Institute of Hospitality is a professional body. A professional body is a group that helps the workers of one industry. It speaks for people like us."

"Three things," said Zohaib. "It watches our standards. Standards mean how good our work must be. It checks that I keep learning every year. They call that CPD, continuing professional development. And it shares best practice. Best practice means the best known way to do a job. Last month I did a food safety course. Next month I do a customer care course."
"You still take courses? You are the manager."
"Yes, because I am the manager. When learning stops, standards drop."
Two weeks later, Mehak learned what standards meant. There was a big wedding. Four hundred guests. At eight o'clock, everything happened at once.

Table twelve wanted more naan. A child spilled a full glass of Rooh Afza. It went on the bride's aunt. The photographer stood in front of the food line. And an angry uncle complained loudly. He said his table was near the stage before.
Mehak froze for one second. Then she remembered Zohaib's training. "Breathe. Do the most urgent thing first."
The spill first. The aunt was wet and upset. Then the angry uncle. Mehak used a calm voice. She found him a better chair. Then naan for table twelve. Then a polite word to the photographer.
Four problems. One girl. Eleven minutes. After it, her hands shook. But her face stayed calm the whole time. A guest told Zohaib, "That young waitress is special. Nothing shakes her."

At closing time, Zohaib made tea for the staff. "You did well," he said. "You stayed calm under pressure. We call that patience under pressure. A calm worker makes the guests calm too. And you did many jobs at once. You chose the most urgent one first. We call that multi-tasking and prioritising."

"Do you see what this job gives you?" he went on. "Work here one year, and you can talk to anyone. You solve problems fast. You talk with angry uncles until they are calm. That skill is called negotiation.
These skills go with you to every job. They help in your own home too. Serve with the right niyyah. Then even carrying naan is worship."
Mehak looked at the certificate on the wall. She made a quiet promise. "One day," she thought, "my name will hang there too."

stories.title: Bilal's Burger Cart
stories.summary: Bilal runs a burger cart alone as a sole trader. He keeps every rupee of profit, but he also carries unlimited liability and the whole workload. When he compares his position with a partnership and then an LLP, the trade-off between control, risk and credibility becomes concrete.
paragraphs: Bilal was nineteen. He saved money for two years. Eid money. Money from teaching. Money from small jobs.

Thirty thousand rupees sat in an envelope. He kept it under his mattress. With it, he bought a small burger cart. It was second-hand. One wheel was loose. He painted it himself. He parked it near the college gates.
Now Bilal was a sole trader. A sole trader owns a business alone. The words felt big. Every rupee of profit was his. Every decision was his too.
Open at four or at five? His choice. The chutney recipe? His secret. He had no boss.

But every problem was his too. One night, the gas cylinder leaked. He smelled it just in time. The repair man came at midnight. He charged double. Bilal paid from his own pocket. There was no other pocket.

His father found him at the kitchen table. Bilal was counting money. He looked sad. His father said, "Listen carefully, beta. Maybe this cart fails one day. Maybe it leaves debts. A debt is money you must pay back. The debt does not stay at the cart. It follows you home. Your savings. Even your motorbike. That is called unlimited liability. The law sees you and the business as one body."
The business grew anyway. Everyone talked about the chutney. Soon twenty students stood in the queue. Bilal cooked, wrapped, and took money all at once.
Orders got mixed up. One evening he gave a boy the wrong change. He only saw it at home. He was tired all the time. He could not do it all alone.

His friend Danish watched him one evening. Bilal had too much work. Danish rolled up his sleeves. "Make me a real partner," Danish said. "I have forty thousand saved. And I am free after Asr every day."

So they became a partnership. A partnership means two or more people own a business together. Danish's money bought a second hotplate. Danish was good at math. He fixed the accounts. They shared the work. They shared their skills. Bilal finally slept well.
But they shared the profit too. Half and half. And one evening they had a bad fight. It happened in front of customers.

Danish wanted to sell fries. "Every cart sells fries. Easy money." Bilal said no. "We are a burger cart. Fries will make the line slow." They did not speak for two days. Partners must agree. But agreeing is hard when both are the boss.
One day a man in a suit came. He had a folder and a big smile. "Boys, you have talent. Do not waste it on a cart with no name. Buy our brand. Join Crunch Burger. Become franchisees."

Bilal did not know that word. The man explained. "A franchise works like this. You pay us. Then you use our big name. We are the franchisor. We own the brand. You are the franchisee. You buy the right to use it. People know our name in six cities. We train you. We give you the recipes. We give you the signboard. We give you our whole system. You cannot fail."
Bilal's heart jumped. A real brand! Then he read the contract slowly. His father taught him that.

There was a big fee at the start. It would take all their savings. There were royalties too. Royalties are payments you send the franchisor every month. A part of every sale, forever. Head office chose the menu. Nobody could change it. Rule nine said: never change any recipe. That rule banned his chutney forever. The whole college queued for that chutney.
Danish spoke quietly. "They give us many things. But they control everything."
They said no, politely. They grew their own name instead.

The cart became a small shop. Then their lawyer gave one more idea. "Register as an LLP," she said. "That means a limited liability partnership. Limited liability means your loss has a limit. Maybe the business fails one day. Then you lose only the money you put in. Your homes stay safe. Your fathers' homes stay safe."
The paperwork took weeks. An accountant checked the accounts every year. He charged real money. It cost more than they liked.
But then the registration came. That night Bilal lay in bed. He felt something new. The business could fail now. His family would still be safe. He slept very well.
Years later, people asked Bilal a question. "Which business type is best?" He always laughed.

"Best for what? Alone, I was fast and free. But I was afraid. With Danish, I was stronger. But we fought. The franchise was safe. But it took away our freedom. The LLP costs me paperwork. But it buys me sleep. Every shape has a price, beta. Know which price you can pay."

quiz.answer: Unlimited liability. As a sole trader the law treats Bilal and the business as one, so if the business owes money his personal savings, and even his motorbike, can be taken to pay the debt. He also carries the whole workload alone and it is hard to cover illness or a day off.

quiz.question: A bank can read an LLP's yearly accounts. A sole trader only gives his word. Why does the bank trust the LLP more?
quiz.answer: Because an LLP must publish yearly accounts, so the bank can see real, checkable evidence of what the business earns and owes. A sole trader offers only his own word, which the bank cannot verify.

quiz.question: What does unlimited liability mean?
quiz.answer: The owner is personally responsible for all business debts; their own savings, car or house can be taken to pay them.

quiz.question: Give two advantages of a partnership.

quiz.question: In a franchise, who is the franchisor?

quiz.question: What does LLP stand for, and what is its big advantage?

quiz.question: Give two examples of hospitality businesses depending on each other.

stories.title: One Chain, Four Names
stories.summary: One late supplier truck ruins an evening at a restaurant called Rabia's, even though the fault lies miles away. The story shows inter-relationships in the industry: hotels, venues, farms, butchers and transport all depend on one another, and the customer blames whoever is standing in front of them.
paragraphs: Rabia owned the Gulshan Marquee. It was the prettiest wedding hall in town. But Rabia sold more than a hall. She sold a promise. "Give me one evening. I will give you a perfect memory."
To keep that promise, she needed other businesses. Saturday's wedding had four hundred guests. She booked everything early.

Faizan's catering company took the cooking job. Chicken qorma, beef pulao, seven dishes. Bushra's flower shop took the stage job. Her roses came from a supplier in Pattoki. A supplier is a business that sells things to other businesses.
Shahid managed the Regal Hotel across the road. He kept twenty rooms for the groom's family. The family was coming from Karachi.
Four businesses, one wedding. Each one needed the others. This is called an inter-relationship. The businesses joined like a chain. Each link held the next link.

Saturday, four o'clock. Rabia's phone rang. It was Faizan. His voice was full of fear. "Rabia baji. My meat supplier's truck broke down. The axle broke near Sahiwal. No beef. No chicken. Nothing came."
Rabia sat down slowly. The wedding started at eight. Four hundred people in their best clothes. They wanted seven dishes.

Rabia did nothing wrong. Faizan did nothing wrong. Even the supplier did nothing wrong. Trucks break sometimes. But at eight o'clock, nobody cares about that. The bride's father paid Rabia. Rabia thought about empty plates. And one sentence in the whole town: "Never book the Gulshan Marquee."
She took one deep breath. Then she started making calls. First she called Shahid at the Regal Hotel. "Shahid bhai, your kitchen buys beef every day. Who is your butcher?"
Shahid answered fast. "I am sending you his number now. Tell him my name. He will open his cold store for you."

Why did he help so fast? Because Shahid needed this wedding too. The groom's family booked twenty rooms in his hotel. They booked them because of Rabia's hall. If the wedding failed, his rooms failed too.

By five thirty, Faizan's vans reached Shahid's butcher. They loaded the meat. The price was higher. Faizan paid the extra without a fight. "Your loss is my loss, baji. We fail together, or we do not fail at all."
Then Bushra called. Her rose supplier sent only half the flowers. The other half died in the heat. Some florists say, "Not my problem." Bushra did not say that.

She drove to two rival flower shops. She bought their flowers at full price. Then she stood on a ladder until seven. She fixed the roses herself. "The stage carries my name too," she said. "Photographers will share my shop's name tonight."

At eight, the guests arrived. The qorma was hot. The stage was full of roses. The Karachi family checked into the Regal Hotel. It was five minutes away. Shahid's receptionist spoke to every guest. She told them about the marquee's Eid brunch. Nobody at the wedding knew about the broken truck.
At midnight, the four of them stood in the empty hall. They drank chai. "One truck," said Faizan. He shook his head. "One broken axle. All four of us almost failed."
Rabia nodded. "That is our trade. We are not four businesses. We are one chain with four names. When one link breaks, every link feels it. Alhamdulillah, tonight the chain held."

stories.title: One Bad Review
stories.lesson_title: The Same High Standard, Every Time
stories.summary: A single bad review sends Zain looking for feedback in six different ways: online reviews, comment cards, surveys, follow-up emails, a mystery shopper and simply talking to guests. He discovers that the customers who say nothing are the dangerous ones, because they leave without ever telling him why.
paragraphs: Zain was twenty-four. He was the new manager of Karavan Grill. His first Monday began with a shock. There was a one-star review online. A review is a note a customer writes about a business. Online reviews are public. Everyone can read them. This one said: "Amazing food on Saturday. Terrible food on Tuesday. Same dish, different restaurant. Never again."

His waitress Amna was angry. "Delete it. Or reply and defend us." Zain shook his head. "No. This review is feedback. Feedback means what customers tell us about our service. This review is a free improvement plan. Someone paid us. Then they showed us our weakness. Most unhappy customers never come back. They say nothing to us. They tell their friends everything. This person took time to write."
But one review is one voice. Zain wanted the full picture. So he collected feedback in many ways, one way at a time.

First, he read every online review from last year. There were two hundred. He made two lists: praise and complaints. Then he put comment cards on the tables. A comment card is a small printed card. Guests write their thoughts on it. The first week, only four came back. One card said the fan above table six made a noise. Zain never noticed that fan. Quiet guests see what managers miss.

Next he printed a QR code on every bill. Guests scanned it with their phones. It opened a short survey. A survey asks customers a few set questions. "Was the food hot? Was the service fast? Will you come

back?" Many people answered. People tap what they never say aloud. He also emailed the weekend guests. One short follow-up email each. "Thank you for coming. What is one thing we can do better?" The replies were kind and honest.

Amna watched with folded arms. "What about customers who lie? Some complain to get free food." Zain smiled. "Some will. So I need one more way. One that cannot lie to me." He phoned his cousin in Sahiwal. The staff did not know his face. "Come on Tuesday. Order the karahi. Watch everything. Then tell me the truth." This is called a mystery shopper. A secret guest who watches and reports back. The cousin came, ate, paid, and left. His report was two pages. It hurt to read.

Now Zain saw the pattern clearly. Saturdays were excellent. Tuesdays were sometimes good, sometimes bad. Why? On Saturday the full team worked. They had a briefing before service. A briefing is a short team meeting. It covers the menu, allergies and important guests. On Tuesday, new part- time staff worked. There was no briefing. Nobody taught them the recipes. Nobody told them about allergies or important guests. Each cook made the karahi his own way.

Zain fixed things piece by piece. He made recipe cards for every dish. Exact spice weights. A photo of the correct plate. He set training every two weeks. The 5pm briefing happened every single day. And he made one rule for everyone. Never promise a guest what the kitchen has not confirmed.

Amna grumbled. "Cards and checklists. Cooking is art, not homework." Zain shrugged. "Art is for the chef's day off. Guests pay for the same dish every time. That is called consistency. The same high standard, every time." Weeks passed. Tuesday food began to taste like Saturday food. The reviews went up. Three stars. Four. Four and a half.

Then Zain did the bravest thing. He wrote to the one-star reviewer. He did not argue at all. He thanked her honestly. He told her what changed. He said her review caused the change. He invited her back as his guest. She came on a Tuesday. She did not trust him yet. The karahi was perfect. Her new review said: "They listened. Five stars."
Zain framed the old one-star review. He hung it in the kitchen. Every cook could see it. Under it he wrote: "Effort is ours. Results belong to Allah. This gift keeps us honest."

quiz.question: Some unhappy customers say nothing. Why is that worse than a complaint?
quiz.answer: Because a complaint is free information that lets you fix the problem. A customer who says nothing simply never returns, tells other people privately, and leaves you with no idea what went wrong, so the same fault keeps costing you customers.

quiz.question: Zain collected feedback in six different ways. Which way told him the most? Why?
quiz.answer: The mystery shopper, because it reports on the service as it actually happens rather than on what customers remember or choose to say afterwards. Reviews and cards only capture the strongest opinions, but a mystery shopper checks the whole standard deliberately.

quiz.question: List five different channels a customer can use to give feedback.
quiz.answer: Any five: comment cards/suggestion boxes; online reviews and social media; surveys and questionnaires (paper, email, QR code); face-to-face comments; complaints or compliments by phone, letter or email; mystery shoppers; follow-up emails.

quiz.question: Why is a silent unhappy customer worse for a business than a complaining one?

quiz.question: What does SOP stand for, and what problem do SOPs solve?
